Carved
KARVD
v.t. (pret. & pp.)
From Anglo-Saxon ceorfan, to cut, to hew. Webster 1828: cut into fanciful figures; engraved; sculptured. In Scripture the carved image is the second commandment’s standing offence, and the skill of the carver is never in doubt.

Biblical Definition

The carved image is the recurring object of Israel’s ruin, and Scripture never suggests it was crude. Micah’s house held a whole apparatus of devotion: these went into Micah's house, and fetched the carved image, the ephod, and the teraphim, and the molten image (Judges 18:18) — note that the ephod, a legitimate priestly garment, is in the same inventory as the idol, which is how syncretism always looks. Manasseh took the offence to its furthest point: he set a carved image, the idol which he had made, in the house of God, of which God had said... In this house, and in Jerusalem... will I put my name for ever (2 Chronicles 33:7). The image is placed in the very house God had named for Himself. Moses commands the opposite treatment: ye shall destroy their altars, and break down their images, and cut down their groves, and burn their graven images with fire (Deuteronomy 7:5). The word also appears innocently, of ordinary furnishing, in the mouth of the strange woman: I have decked my bed with coverings of tapestry, with carved works, with fine linen of Egypt (Proverbs 7:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines CARVE as to cut into fanciful figures; to make by cutting, as an image; to engrave; hence CARVED, cut into shapes or figures; sculptured; engraved.

expand to see more

CARVE, v.t. — To cut into fanciful figures; to make by cutting; as, to carve an image.

To engrave; to cut into a surface, as letters or figures.

To cut, as meat at table; to distribute in portions.

CARVED, pp. — Cut into images or figures; engraved; sculptured.

Anglo-Saxon ceorfan, to cut — related to carve, kerf, and Greek grapho, to cut or write.

Key Scripture

Judges 18:18 — "And these went into Micah's house, and fetched the carved image, the ephod, and the teraphim, and the molten image. Then said the priest unto them, What do ye?"

2 Chronicles 33:7 — "And he set a carved image, the idol which he had made, in the house of God, of which God had said to David and to Solomon his son, In this house, and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen before all the tribes of Israel, will I put my name for ever:"

Deuteronomy 7:5 — "But thus shall ye deal with them; ye shall destroy their altars, and break down their images, and cut down their groves, and burn their graven images with fire."

Proverbs 7:16 — "I have decked my bed with coverings of tapestry, with carved works, with fine linen of Egypt."

Modern Corruption

The second commandment forbids images used in the worship of the true God, not only the worship of false gods, which is the point Rome’s distinction between veneration and adoration is designed to evade.

expand to see more

Micah’s house is the instructive case, because the man was not an atheist and not, in his own mind, an idolater. He had an ephod, a Levite for a priest, and a carved image, and Judges 17:13 records his conclusion: Now know I that the LORD will do me good, seeing I have a Levite to my priest. He was worshipping the LORD by means the LORD had not appointed. That is what the second commandment forbids, and it is distinct from the first: the first forbids other gods, the second forbids images in the worship of the true God. Rome’s answer — that images receive dulia or veneration rather than latria or adoration, and that the honour passes to the prototype — is a distinction the commandment does not make, and it is worth noting that the Roman catechetical tradition has commonly numbered the commandments so that this one disappears into the first.

Manasseh’s carved image in the temple is the extreme case, and Chronicles is careful to record God’s own words about that house before describing what was set in it. The narrative is also, remarkably, a story of grace: 2 Chronicles 33:12-13 says that in his affliction Manasseh besought the LORD, humbled himself greatly, and was heard and restored. The most flagrant idolater in Judah’s history repented and was received, which is why his account stands as one of Scripture’s strongest evidences that no sinner is beyond mercy. Reformation, when it came under Josiah, still had to remove what Manasseh had built — forgiveness of a man does not undo the consequences of his work in a nation.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pesel (H6459), a carved or graven image; pasal (H6458), to hew or carve; massekah (H4541), a molten image; teraphim (H8655), household idols.

expand to see more

Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a carved or graven image; the object forbidden in the second commandment (Exodus 20:4).

Hebrew pasal (H6458) — to hew, to carve; the verb behind pesel, used also of hewing the second tables of stone.

Hebrew massekah (H4541) — a molten or cast image; the companion of the carved one in Micah’s house (Judges 18:18).

Hebrew teraphim (H8655) — household idols or images; part of the same inventory (Judges 18:18).

Hebrew asherah (H842) — a grove or wooden cult object; commanded to be cut down (Deuteronomy 7:5).

Usage

"The carved image, the ephod, and the teraphim, and the molten image (Judges 18:18) — the legitimate and the forbidden in one inventory."

"He set a carved image... in the house of God (2 Chronicles 33:7) — in the very house God had named for Himself."

"Burn their graven images with fire (Deuteronomy 7:5) — the appointed treatment, and it is not partial."
